newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Hutu faction in Burundi rejects armed struggle.
newsitem.headline: Hutu faction in Burundi rejects armed struggle.

text.p: Officials from one faction of Burundi's main Hutu party, split since an army coup in July, said on Monday they backed exiled president Jean Minani and were committed to solving the conflict with Tutsi rivals peacefully.
The group made the announcement a week after another wing of the Frodebu party elected rebel leader Leonard Nyangoma as its president and endorsed armed struggle.

Frodebu Secretary-General Augustin Nzojibwami said party leaders at the weekend in Bujumbura confirmed their commitment to a peaceful resolution to Burundi's conflict between Hutu rebels and the Tutsi-dominated military and supported Minani.
"Participants reaffirmed that there is no military solution to the Burundian conflict. Only negotiations...will bring peace to Burundi," the party said in a statement after the talks.
Frodebu has been divided since the Tutsi-dominated army seized power on July 25 and Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya ousted Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Frodebu member.
Buyoya suspended all political parties during the coup and many Frodebu members including Minai fled into exile abroad.

Nzojibwami told Reuters on Wednesday several Frodebu leaders who took refuge in the German embassy in Bujumbura after the coup left their sanctuary at the weekend after Buyoya lifted the ban on political parties.
The only two still being protected by foreign powers were Ntibantunganya, who took refuge at the U.S. ambassador's residence, and Leonce Ngendakumana, the former Frodebu parliament speaker.
Sanctions have cut off oil imports to the landlocked country and blocked exports of coffee, its main hard currency earner.
The head of the Roman Catholic Church in Bujumbura said on Saturday unconditional talks between all groups were the only way forward for the ethnically divided central African nation.
But he also said testimony from survivors showed rebels were responsible for killing Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna, the country's senior Catholic prelate, who died in an ambush on September 9.
Buyoya has said he will not talk peace with the rebels -- as demanded by regional powers -- until they give up their arms.
More than 150,000 people -- mostly civilians -- have died in three years of violence between the army and rebels from the Hutu majority, which makes up 85 percent of the country's six million people.
Regional leaders fear Burundi could follow the path of neighbouring Rwanda, where up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were slaughtered in genocidal killings in 1994.
